## CHAPTER 10

## Endocrine Disorders

## CONTENT OVERVIEW

- Diabetes
- Thyroid disorders
- Obesity
- Uncommon endocrine disorders

## NOTES

<!-- image -->

## Classification of Diabetes Mellitus (DM)

- Type 1 DM: caused by autoimmune destruction of beta cells; absolute insulin deficiency
- Type 2 DM: caused by the progressive loss of insulin secretion by beta cells, often with associated insulin resistance
- Gestational DM: diabetes that develops during pregnancy that was not present prior to gestation, diagnosed in the 2nd or 3rd trimester
- Others: latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (LADA), mild obesity-related diabetes (MOD), mild age-related diabetes (MARD)

## Risk Factors for Type 2 DM

| Risk Factors       | Risk Factors                                                                                     |
|--------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Age                | 45 years or older                                                                                |
| BMI                | 25 kg/m 2 or higher ( or ≥23 if Asian American)                                                  |
| Family history     | DM in first-degree relative                                                                      |
| Inactivity         | Sedentary lifestyle                                                                              |
| Medical history    | Dyslipidemia, gestational DM, hyperuricemia, metabolic syndrome, or cardiovascular disease (CVD) |
| Insulin resistance | Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), acanthosis nigricans, severe obesity                           |
| Race               | Black, Latino American, Native American, Asian American, Pacific Islander                        |
| Glucose            | Prior A1c greater than 5.7% (pre-DM), impaired glucose tolerance                                 |

## Screening

## USPSTF Recommendations: Diabetes and Prediabetes Screening USPSTF Recommendations: Diabetes and Prediabetes Screening

<!-- image -->

TIP: If BMI changes, screen sooner.

## ADA Diagnostic Criteria

| Type of Test                                        | Pre-DM         | Type 2 DM            |
|-----------------------------------------------------|----------------|----------------------|
| A1c                                                 | 5.7-6.4%       | 6.5% or greater      |
| FPG                                                 | 100-125 mg/dL  | 126 mg/dL or greater |
| Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)                  | 140-199 mg/dL  | over 200 mg/dL       |
| Random plasma glucose (RPG) with signs and symptoms | Not applicable | over 200 mg/dL       |

Diagnosis should be confirmed with repeat testing unless unequivocal hyperglycemia.

## QUESTION #1

Which statement about the diagnosis of diabetes is true?

1. An A1c of 6.1% is diagnostic of DM.
2. Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) means nothing to eat or drink in the last 4 hours.
3. A FPG of 160 mg/dL and an A1c of 6.6% is diagnostic.
4. A postprandial plasma glucose (PPG) of more than 200 mg/dL is diagnostic.

## Prediabetes Management

Lifestyle Modifications

- All patients
- $ Weight loss ≥7% can prevent diabetes.
- $ Reduced calorie diet
- $ 150 minutes per week of moderate activity

## Consider Metformin

- Select patients
- $ A1c 6-6.4%
- $ ≤60 and BMI ≥35
- $ Personal history of gestational diabetes
- $ FPG ≥110 mg/dL

## QUESTION #2

Each of these patients has an A1c goal of 7% or less. Which patient would benefit most from an A1c adjustment?

1. An older patient who has been controlled on their oral medications for 5 years
2. A patient with advanced CVD who has frequent episodes of hypoglycemia
3. A medically complex patient whose HbA1c is stable at 6.9% on the current regimen
4. An adult who is well controlled on oral meds but has been diagnosed with early Alzheimer's disease

- Fasting blood glucose
- $ Healthy patients:
- 80-130 mg/dL
- $ Frail patients:
- Less stringent
- Postprandial glucose
- $ 2 hours after a meal
- $ <180 mg/dL

## Diabetes Monitoring

| Measure             | Frequency                                      | Comments                                                                                    |
|---------------------|------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| A1c                 | Every 3 months until goal; then every 6 months | · The better the control, the better the reduction in micro and macrovascular complications |
| Lipids              | At diagnosis and annually                      | · Establish cardiovascular risk (ASCVD). · Initiate statin based on risk. · See next slide. |
| Height, weight, BMI | Every visit                                    | · Lifestyle modifications to reduce weight                                                  |
| Blood pressure      | Every visit                                    | · Target BP ≤130/80 mm Hg · Consider ACE/ARB in patients with proteinuria or CAD.           |

## Diabetes Drug Classes

| Drug Class                    | Suffix         | Examples                                                      |
|-------------------------------|----------------|---------------------------------------------------------------|
| Biguanide                     | Not Applicable | Metformin                                                     |
| Sulfonylurea (2nd generation) | -ride/-zide    | Glimepiride, glipizide, glyburide                             |
| Meglitinides                  | -glinide       | Repaglinide, nateglinide                                      |
| DPP-4 inhibitor               | -gliptin       | Alogliptin, linagliptin, saxagliptin, sitagliptin             |
| GLP-1                         | -atide/-utide  | Exenatide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, albiglutide, semaglutide |
| Thiazolidinedione (TZD)       | -azone         | Pioglitazone, rosiglitazone                                   |
| SGLT-2                        | -gliflozin     | Canagliflozin, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin                   |
| GIP/GLP-1                     | -tide          | Tirzepatide                                                   |

TIP: Memorize the characteristics and suffixes of each drug class.

## Medication Summary

| Class                       | Mechanism of Action                                                   | A1c Decrease   | Comment                                             | Cost/Month   |
|-----------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------|-----------------------------------------------------|--------------|
| GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist  | Increases insulin synthesis in response to hyperglycemia              | 1.7-2.4%       | Weight loss, CV benefit, possible renal benefit     | $1200        |
| GLP-1 receptor agonist      | Increases insulin synthesis in response to blood glucose rise         | 0.5-1.5%       | Weight loss, CV benefit, possible renal benefit     | $800-$1200   |
| Insulin (human and analogs) | Replaces insulin deficits                                             | 1.5-3.5%       | Weight gain, decrease in eGFR requires lower dosing | $24-$1200    |
| Biguanide                   | Decreases glucose production/absorption; improves insulin sensitivity | 1-2%           | No hypoglycemia, weight neutral, caution with CKD   | CHEAP!       |
| Sulfonylureas               | Increases insulin secretion                                           | 1-2%           | Hypoglycemia, weight gain                           | CHEAP!       |

## NOTES

## NOTES Medication Summary (cont.)

| Name              | Mechanism of Action                                      | A1c Decrease   | Comment                                                      | Cost/Month   |
|-------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|----------------|--------------------------------------------------------------|--------------|
| SGLT-2 inhibitors | Prevents renal glucose reabsorption                      | 0.5-0.8%       | Weight loss, reduces BP; can cause UTI, yeast infections     | $400-$700    |
| TZDs              | Improves insulin sensitivity                             | 0.5-1.4%       | Contraindicated in heart failure; increased risk of fracture | $300-$400    |
| DPP-4             | Slows inactivation of incretin (decreases blood glucose) | 0.5-0.8%       | Not first-line; GI effects, pancreatitis                     | $200-$600    |

## Type 2 DM: First Medication

- Metformin is often the first medication choice.
- $ Effective (lowers A1c 1-2%)
- $ Inexpensive/widely available
- $ Reduces cardiovascular risk
- $ Well tolerated
- $ Weight neutral
- GLP-1 or GLP-1/GIP, SGLT-2 can be started first-line if:
- $ The patient meets certain characteristics (obesity, high ASCVD risk, CKD).

## QUESTION #9

A patient takes an SGLT-2, a GLP-1, and metformin but is still not to their A1c goal. Which of the options is a reasonable next step?

1. Add meal-time insulin to the current regimen.
2. Add basal insulin and discontinue metformin.
3. Add basal insulin and discontinue the GLP-1.
4. Add basal insulin to the current regimen.

## When to Consider Basal Insulin

- Early use can preserve pancreatic function.
- Consider in patients with:
- $ A1c ≥ 10% or FPG ≥ 300 mg/dL
- $ Symptoms of hyperglycemia
- $ Severe hyperglycemia with ketonuria
- $ After maxing out orals/injectables
- $ Pregnant patients
- $ Ongoing catabolism (unexpected weight loss)

<!-- image -->

TIP: In DM2, the ADA recommends trying a GLP-1 or GLP-1/GIP before insulin whenever possible!

## ADA Recommendations for Managing Insulin, 2025

<!-- image -->

*Basal coverage may be inadequate if the patient requires more than 0.5 u/kg/day, if there is a wide difference between bedtime/morning, or elevated FPG/postprandial glucose levels, or if hypoglycemia.

<!-- image -->

|-------|-----------|
|     1 | 150 mg/dL |
|     2 | 144 mg/dL |
|     3 | 156 mg/dL |

1. Decrease the dose by 2 units.
2. Continue the same dose.
3. Increase the dose by 3 units.
4. Add 3 units of am insulin to current regimen.

## QUESTION #11

A patient takes 40 units of basal insulin and has an average FBG of 110 mg/dL. The patient's postprandial glucose is over 200 mg/dL. Mealtime insulin will be prescribed. Which choice is most appropriate?

1. Add 2 units of basal insulin with the largest meal of the day.
2. Add 2 units rapid-acting insulin with the largest meal of the day.
3. Add 4 units basal insulin with every meal.
4. Add 4 units rapid-acting insulin with the largest meal of the day.

## THYROID DISORDERS

## Thyroid Pathophysiology

Functional problems

- Hypothyroidism
- $ Primary
- $ Subclinical
- $ Secondary
- Hyperthyroidism
- $ Primary
- $ Subclinical
- $ Secondary

Structural problems

- Goiter-enlargement
- Thyroiditis-inflammation
- Nodules
- $ Benign
- $ Toxic nodules
- $ Thyroid cancer

<!-- image -->

Joshua Lanclos/APEA

TIP: Structural thyroid problems can cause functional problems!

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Thyroid Hormones

<!-- image -->

## Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH)

- TSH is the most sensitive measure of thyroid function.
- $ TSH is the "early warning system".
- $ Changes in TSH levels occur before changes in T3/T4.
- $ More reliable than T3 and T4 levels
- $ A small change in circulating T3/T4 results in a very large change in TSH.
- TSH measurement is clinically useful.
- $ To screen for thyroid disorders
- $ To monitor thyroid hormone supplementation

## Thyroid Hormones-T3 and T4

| T4-Thyroxine (Tetraiodothyronine) 4 Iodine Atoms   | T3-Triiodothyronine 3 iodine Atoms                                        |
|----------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 80% released by thyroid                            | 20% produced by thyroid; majority converted from T4 in peripheral tissues |
| Free T4-Active                                     | 99.5% is bound and inactive                                               |
| More specific to hypothyroidism                    | More specific to hyperthyroidism                                          |

<!-- image -->

## Hypothyroidism

| Thyroid State              | TSH               | Free T4               | T3                         |
|----------------------------|-------------------|-----------------------|----------------------------|
| Euthyroid                  | Normal            | Normal                | Normal                     |
| Primary hypothyroidism     | Increased         | Decreased             | Normal (Usually) Manage in |
| Subclinical hypothyroidism | Increased         | Normal                | Normal Primary Care        |
| Secondary hypothyroidism   | Normal/ Decreased | Decreased/ Low-Normal | Normal/Decreased Refer     |

- Primary: problem with thyroid (e.g., autoimmune disorder)
- Secondary: problem originates outside the thyroid; may have other hormonal abnormalities; feedback loop failure

## Subclinical Hypothyroidism

- Labs: increased TSH, normal free T4
- $ TSH greater than 10 mU/L
- Treat to prevent progression to primary hypothyroidism.
- Prescribe 25 to 50 mcg or 1.6 mcg/kg/day IBW.
- $ TSH less than 10 mU/L
- Treatment usually not beneficial
- Recheck TSH in 6 to 12 months or if symptoms increase.

## QUESTION #12

Mrs. B, age 42, reports fatigue and weight gain. Her TSH level is elevated to 7 mIU/L (normal: 0.5-4.0 mIU/L). T4 level is normal. Based on these results, what is the diagnosis and best action by the NP?

1. Hypothyroidism; initiate levothyroxine
2. Subclinical hypothyroidism; repeat the TSH in 6-12 months.
3. Subclinical hypothyroidism; initiate levothyroxine
4. Subclinical hypothyroidism; initiate Armour Thyroid

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #13

Mrs. B, age 42, returns for follow-up in a year with these lab values. What should be done next?

|                  | TSH           | Free T4        |
|------------------|---------------|----------------|
| Reported value   | 15 mIU/L      | 0.3 mIU/L      |
| Reference ranges | 0.5-4.0 mIU/L | 0.7-1.53 mIU/L |

1. Continue monitoring the TSH in 6-12 months.
2. Calculate ideal body weight (IBW) and prescribe levothyroxine.
3. Evaluate for secondary causes of hypothyroidism.
4. Order thyroid antibody studies.

<!-- image -->

## NOTES

## NOTES Primary Hypothyroidism

- Primary-problem with the thyroid (over 95%)
- Usually caused by an autoimmune conditionHashimoto thyroiditis
- $ Antibody studies not high-yielding
- Risk factors: family hx, increasing age, female sex

Confirmatory diagnostics: increased TSH, decreased free T4

## Initial Levothyroxine Dosing

Who is your patient?

| Age/Health Status                                    | Initial Dose                              |
|------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Under age 50, healthy                                | 1.6 mcg/kg of ideal body weight (IBW)/day |
| Age 50-60, mild to moderate health issues            | 50 mcg/day                                |
| Over age 60, cardiac issues or serious comorbidities | 25 mcg/day                                |

<!-- image -->

TIP: start low, go slow!

## QUESTION #14

The following patients have primary hypothyroidism. What initial levothyroxine dose should be prescribed in each patient?

| Patient                    | Calculated Dose   | Starting Dose   |
|----------------------------|-------------------|-----------------|
| 55-year-old with OA        | 87 mcg            |                 |
| 72-year-old with HTN       | 112 mcg           |                 |
| 28-year-old with asthma    | 116 mcg           |                 |
| 46-year-old healthy female | 96 mcg            |                 |

Available Tablet Doses (mcg):

25, 50, 75, 88, 100, 112, 125, 137, 150, 175, 200, 300

## Levothyroxine Dose Titration

## To achieve euthyroid

- Check TSH every 4 to 8 weeks until euthyroid.
- TSH ≥4.0 mIU/L
- Increase levothyroxine to next available dosage.

## Once stable

- Monitor TSH only.
- Annually
- Major changes in health status

<!-- image -->

## QUESTION #15

A patient has taken 88 mcg of levothyroxine daily for the past 6 weeks. The patient's TSH has decreased from 28 mIU/L to 8 mIU/L and the patient feels much better. What should be done next?

1. Continue current levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH in 6 months.
2. Order a free T4 level to inform decision-making.
3. Increase levothyroxine dose and recheck TSH in 4-6 weeks.
4. Prescribe combination T3/T4 therapy.

## Patient Education About Levothyroxine

- Levothyroxine is a picky drug!
- $ Must take with water on an empty stomach
- $ Interacts with other medications
- Hypothyroidism control affected by
- $ Weight change of 10% or more
- $ Taking levothyroxine with food or other meds
- $ Missed or extra medication doses
- $ Use of antiepileptic drugs, steroids
- $ Pregnancy (increases needs 30%)
- $ Biotin interferes with measurement of TSH

## Hyperthyroidism

- Presentation
- $ Heat intolerance, warm and moist skin
- $ Fine tremor in hands
- $ Tachycardia or tachyarrhythmias
- $ Anxiety, irritability
- $ Ophthalmopathy-early or late finding in Graves disease

## Hyperthyroidism

<!-- image -->

Refer all patients with hyperthyroidism!

| Thyroid State               | TSH              | Free T4          | T3        |
|-----------------------------|------------------|------------------|-----------|
| Euthyroid                   | Normal           | Normal           | Normal    |
| Primary hyperthyroidism     | Decreased        | Increased/Normal | Increased |
| Subclinical hyperthyroidism | Decreased        | Normal           | Normal    |
| Secondary hyperthyroidism   | Normal/Increased | Increased        | Increased |

TIP: Nonspecific beta-blockers (e.g., propranolol) may be prescribed for symptom management while awaiting endocrinology referral.

## Obesity Screening

United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends identifying adults with a BMI over 30

## Screening Measures

- Body mass index (BMI)
- Waist circumference Over 40 inches for males Over 35 inches for females

| BMI          | Classification    |
|--------------|-------------------|
| 25-29.9      | Overweight        |
| 30-34.9      | Class I obesity   |
| 35-39.9      | Class II obesity  |
| 40 or higher | Class III obesity |

## Approach to Overweight and Obesity Management

| Patient Category                | Initial Labs                                               | Goal/Strategies                                                                                               |
|---------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| BMI 25-29.9, no comorbidities   | · A1c · Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)                  | · Prevent further weight gain and comorbidities. · Lifestyle modifications-healthy diet and physical activity |
| BMI 27-29.9, with comorbidities | · Liver enzymes · Fasting lipids · Others based on history | · Weight loss · Structured behavioral modification · Pharmacotherapy for some patients                        |
| BMI 30-34.4                     |                                                            | · As above, plus · Pharmacotherapy for most patients                                                          |
| BMI 35 or higher                |                                                            | · As above, plus · Bariatric surgery may be considered                                                        |

## Indications for Obesity Medications

Indications for pharmacologic therapy

| BMI 27-29.9                    | BMI over 30                                      |
|--------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| · With comorbidities (DM, HTN) | · BMI alone often warrants pharmacologic therapy |

⎫⎪⎪⎪⎬⎪⎪⎪⎭

Not successful with lifestyle alone Success = ≥5% of TBW loss Sustained by 3 to 6 months

TIP: Lifestyle interventions continue during medical or surgical therapy.

## OVERWEIGHT AND OBESITY

## FDA-Approved Medications for Weight Loss

| Medications                                                                         | Average Weight Loss   | Comments                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Tirzepatide (Zepbound) · GLP-1/GIP dual receptor agonist · Weekly SQ injection      | 15-20%                | · Probable ASCVD protection; lowers glucose · Avoid if history of pancreatitis, endocrine tumors. · GI side effects limit tolerance; titrate to max dose. · Very expensive, insurance may not cover · Weight regain upon discontinuation |
| Semaglutide (Wegovy) Liraglutide (Saxenda) · GLP-1 receptor agonists · SQ injection | 8-14%                 | · ASCVD protection, lowers glucose · Avoid if history of pancreatitis, endocrine tumors. · GI side effects limit tolerance; titrate to max dose. · Very expensive, insurance may not cover · Weight regain upon discontinuation          |
| Phentermine-Topiramate · Stimulant/anticonvulsant                                   | 9%                    | · Topiramate increases risk of birth. · Increases HR, risk of neuropsychiatric disturbances · DEA category C-IV                                                                                                                          |
| Orlistat · Lipase inhibitor                                                         | 6%                    | · Improve lipids, BP, glucose control · GI side effects significantly limit use (steatorrhea).                                                                                                                                           |
| Bupropion-naltrexone · NDRI/opiate antagonist                                       | 5 to 6%               | · May increase BP and heart rate · Avoid in seizure disorder, severe HTN.                                                                                                                                                                |

## Uncommon Endocrine Conditions

| Disorder                                  | Typical Presentation                                                      | Pathophysiology                                                                              | Management                                       |
|-------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| Addison's disease (Adrenal Insufficiency) | Fatigue, vomiting, weight loss, skin, postural hypotension                | Inadequate cortisol, aldosterone, androgens production                                       | Corticosteroid, fludrocortisone supplements      |
| Cushing disease                           | Moon face, buffalo hump, central adiposity, striae                        | Excess cortisol production by adrenal tumor                                                  | Surgery to remove adrenal tumor, radiation, meds |
| Cushing syndrome                          | Moon face, buffalo hump, central adiposity, striae                        | Elevated cortisol levels due to corticosteroid use                                           | Wean corticosteroid drugs if possible            |
| Primary hyper- parathyroidism             | Asymptomatic, elevated serum calcium and parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels | Overactive parathyroid gland produces excess PTH, pulling calcium from bones into the serum. | Surgical removal of overactive parathyroid gland |
